Since the set [MATH: \{f_1(t),f_2(t)\}] is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of [MATH: g(t)] onto the subspace [MATH: S] is given by

[MATH: \textrm{proj}_{S}\,g(t) = \textrm{proj}_{f_1(t)}\,g(t) + \textrm{proj}_{f_2(t)}\,g(t).]

We are given that [MATH: \textrm{proj}_{f_1(t)}\,g(t) = 2,] so let's now find the orthogonal projection of [MATH: g(t)] onto [MATH: \textrm{Span}\{f_2(t)\}.] This can be computed as

[MATH: \textrm{proj}_{f_2(t)}\,g(t) = \dfrac{\langle{g(t),f_2(t)}\rangle}{\langle{f_2(t),f_2(t)}\rangle}\,f_2(t).]

In our case, we have

[MATH: ⟨g(t), f_{2}(t)⟩|= ∫_{− 1}^{1}g(t)f_{2}(t)dt; = ∫_{− 1}^{1}6t^{2} ⋅ \sin (πt)dt; = ∫_{− 1}^{1}6t^{2}\sin (πt)dt.]

Notice that [MATH: \sin (\pi t)] is an odd function, while [MATH: 6t^2] is even. Hence, their product [MATH: 6 t^2 \sin (\pi t)] must be an odd function. Now, since we have an integral over the interval [MATH: [-1,1],] which is symmetric about the origin, we can conclude that

[MATH: \int_{-1}^{1} 6t^2 \sin (\pi t) \, \text{d}t = 0.]

Therefore,

[MATH: \textrm{proj}_{f_2(t)}\,g(t) = \dfrac{0}{\langle{f_2(t),f_2(t)}\rangle} \cdot \sin \pi t = 0.]

Finally,

[MATH: proj_{S}g(t)|= proj_{f_{1}(t)}g(t) + proj_{f_{2}(t)}g(t); = 2 + 0; = 2.]

is a set of mutually orthogonal vectors in [MATH: V,] then the orthogonal projection of a vector [MATH: \mathbf{x}\in V] onto the subspace

Content:
[MATH: S = \textrm{Span}\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 , \ldots, \mathbf{a}_n \}]
with respect to the inner product is given by

Content:
[MATH: proj_{S}x|= proj_{a_{1}}x + proj_{a_{2}}x + ⋯ + proj_{a_{n}}x; = (⟨x, a_{1}⟩)/(⟨a_{1}, a_{1}⟩)a_{1} + (⟨x, a_{2}⟩)/(⟨a_{2}, a_{2}⟩)a_{2} + ⋯ + (⟨x, a_{n}⟩)/(⟨a_{n}, a_{n}⟩)a_{n}.]

Content:
In other words, the orthogonal projection of [MATH: \mathbf{x}] onto [MATH: S] is the sum of the orthogonal projections of [MATH: \mathbf{x}] onto each one-dimensional subspace [MATH: \textrm{Span}\big\{ \mathbf{a}_i\}] for [MATH: i=1, 2, \cdots, n.]

Content:
Note the following:

Content:
- This is entirely analogous to the corresponding formula for Euclidean spaces.
- As in Euclidean spaces, the formula works only when the set of vectors [MATH: \{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 , \ldots, \mathbf{a}_n \}] is orthogonal with respect to the inner product!

Item 2 — Tutorial: A Worked Example

Consider the functions

Content:
in the vector space [MATH: V = \mathcal{C}[-1,1]] of continuous functions over [MATH: [-1,1],] where the inner product is defined as

Content:
[MATH: \langle x(t),y(t) \rangle = \int_{-1}^1 x(t) y(t) \, \text{d}t.]

Content:
[MATH: S= \textrm{Span}\{f_1(t), f_2(t)\},]

given that [MATH: f_1(t) \perp f_2(t)] with respect to this inner product.

Content:
Since the set [MATH: \{f_1(t),f_2(t)\}] is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of [MATH: h(t)] onto [MATH: S] is given by

Content:
[MATH: \textrm{proj}_{S}\,h(t)
= \textrm{proj}_{f_1(t)}\,h(t) + \textrm{proj}_{f_2(t)}\,h(t).]

Content:
Let's now compute these projections:

Content:

[MATH: proj_{f_{1}(t)}h(t)|= (⟨h(t), f_{1}(t)⟩)/(⟨f_{1}(t), f_{1}(t)⟩)f_{1}(t); = (∫_{− 1}^{1}5t^{4}dt)/(∫_{− 1}^{1}t^{2}dt) ⋅ t; = 3t]
- Next, we compute the orthogonal projection of [MATH: h(t)] onto [MATH: \textrm{Span}\{f_2(t)\}\mathbin{:}]
[MATH: proj_{f_{2}(t)}h(t)|= (⟨h(t), f_{2}(t)⟩)/(⟨f_{2}(t), f_{2}(t)⟩)f_{2}(t); = (∫_{− 1}^{1}5t^{3}(t^{2} + 1)dt)/(∫_{− 1}^{1}(t^{2} + 1)^{2}dt) ⋅ (t^{2} + 1); = 0.]
Note: We used the fact that the integrand in the numerator is an odd function, so its integral over [MATH: [-1,1]] must be zero.

Content:
Finally, we have

Content:
[MATH: proj_{S}h(t)|= proj_{f_{1}(t)}h(t) + proj_{f_{2}(t)}h(t); = 3t + 0; = 3t.]

Item 6 — Example: Finding the Orthogonal Projection of a Vector Onto a Subspace Spanned by Orthogonal Vectors

Example Prompt:

[MATH: f_1(t)=1,\quad f_2(t)=\sin \pi t, \quad g(t)=6t^2]

Find the orthogonal projection of [MATH: g(t)] onto [MATH: S=\text{Span}\{f_1(t), f_2(t)\}] given that [MATH: f_1(t) \perp f_2(t)] with respect to the inner product, and that the orthogonal projection of [MATH: g(t)] onto [MATH: \textrm{Span}\{f_1(t)\}] equals [MATH: 2.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Since the set [MATH: \{f_1(t),f_2(t)\}] is orthogonal, the orthogonal projection of [MATH: g(t)] onto the subspace [MATH: S] is given by

[MATH: \textrm{proj}_{S}\,g(t)
= \textrm{proj}_{f_1(t)}\,g(t) + \textrm{proj}_{f_2(t)}\,g(t).]

We are given that [MATH: \textrm{proj}_{f_1(t)}\,g(t) = 2,] so let's now find the orthogonal projection of [MATH: g(t)] onto [MATH: \textrm{Span}\{f_2(t)\}.] This can be computed as

[MATH: \textrm{proj}_{f_2(t)}\,g(t)
= \dfrac{\langle{g(t),f_2(t)}\rangle}{\langle{f_2(t),f_2(t)}\rangle}\,f_2(t).]

In our case, we have

[MATH: ⟨g(t), f_{2}(t)⟩|= ∫_{− 1}^{1}g(t)f_{2}(t)dt; = ∫_{− 1}^{1}6t^{2} ⋅ \sin (πt)dt; = ∫_{− 1}^{1}6t^{2}\sin (πt)dt.]

Notice that [MATH: \sin (\pi t)] is an odd function, while [MATH: 6t^2] is even. Hence, their product [MATH: 6 t^2 \sin (\pi t)] must be an odd function. Now, since we have an integral over the interval [MATH: [-1,1],] which is symmetric about the origin, we can conclude that

[MATH: \int_{-1}^{1} 6t^2 \sin (\pi t) \, \text{d}t = 0.]

Therefore,

[MATH: \textrm{proj}_{f_2(t)}\,g(t) = \dfrac{0}{\langle{f_2(t),f_2(t)}\rangle} \cdot \sin \pi t = 0.]

Finally,

[MATH: proj_{S}g(t)|= proj_{f_{1}(t)}g(t) + proj_{f_{2}(t)}g(t); = 2 + 0; = 2.]

Item 9 — Tutorial: The Distance Between a Vector and a Subspace

Content:
Suppose that [MATH: V] is a vector space equipped with an inner product [MATH: \left\langle\cdot, \cdot\right\rangle] and that [MATH: \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{w} \in V.] The distance [MATH: d] between [MATH: \mathbf v] and [MATH: \mathbf w] with respect to the inner product is given by the norm of [MATH: \mathbf{v}- \mathbf{w}.] That is,

Content:
[MATH: d|= ‖v − w‖ = sqrt(⟨v − w, v − w⟩).]

Content:
For example, suppose that [MATH: V = \mathcal{C}[0,1],] the vector space of continuous functions over [MATH: [0,1],] equipped with the inner product

Content:
[MATH: \langle x(t),y(t) \rangle = \int_0^{1} x(t) y(t) \, \text{d}t.]

Content:
The distance between the functions [MATH: f(t)=4t] and [MATH: g(t)=t+1] with respect to the given inner product is

Content:
[MATH: d|= ‖f(t) − g(t)‖; = ‖4t − (t + 1)‖; = ‖3t − 1‖; = sqrt(⟨3t − 1, 3t − 1⟩); = sqrt(∫_{0}^{1}(3t − 1)^{2}dt); = sqrt((1)/(9) ⋅ (3t − 1)^{3}|_{0}^{1}); = sqrt((1)/(9) ⋅ [(8) − (− 1)]); = sqrt((1)/(9) ⋅ 9); = sqrt(1); = 1.]

Content:
More generally, given an orthogonal set

Content:
[MATH: \big\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 , \ldots, \mathbf{a}_n \big\} \subset V]
and a vector [MATH: \mathbf x \in V,] the distance between [MATH: \mathbf{x}] and the subspace

Content:
[MATH: S=\textrm{Span}\{ \mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2, \ldots, \mathbf{a}_n \}]
is defined as

Content:
[MATH: \Vert{ \color{black} \mathbf{x} - \text{proj}_{S}\,\mathbf{x} }\Vert.]

[MATH: d|= ‖p(t) − proj_{q(t)}p(t)‖; = ‖(4t + 2) − 6t‖; = ‖ − 2t + 2‖; = sqrt(⟨ − 2t + 2, − 2t + 2⟩).]

Item 13 — Tutorial: The Intuition Behind Orthogonal Projections in Inner Product Spaces

Content:
The orthogonal projection of a vector [MATH: \mathbf{x}\in V] onto [MATH: \textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}\}] (or simply onto a vector [MATH: \mathbf{a}]) is the vector [MATH: \text{proj}_{\mathbf{a}}\,\mathbf{x}\in \textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}\}] that is "closest" to [MATH: \mathbf{x}] with respect to the distance defined by the inner product.

Content:
As shown in the diagram, the projection of [MATH: \mathbf{x}] onto [MATH: \textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}\}] is the vector [MATH: \text{proj}_{\mathbf{a}}\,\mathbf{x}] such that [MATH: \mathbf{x} - \text{proj}_{\mathbf{a}}\,\mathbf{x}] is orthogonal to [MATH: \textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}\}.]

Furthermore, [MATH: \| \mathbf{x} - \text{proj}_{\mathbf{a}}\,\mathbf{x} \|] will be the smallest possible distance (with respect to our inner product) from [MATH: \mathbf{x}] to any vector in [MATH: \textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}\}.]
